observed_publication: Published Feb 22 (year not shown in UI)
observation: Authenticated Safari accessibility content, October 18, 2026, America/Los_Angeles. Original excerpts transcribed; cover image was not fact-checked. No live edits, unpublishing, or republishing performed.

claims.original_excerpt: They operate at different layers of the GPU execution stack
claims.finding: Useful distinction: submission versus device implementation. Layers interact and techniques can be combined.

claims.original_excerpt: Application layer — Python/C++ framework logic (PyTorch, vLLM)
claims.finding: A useful explanatory abstraction, not an official exhaustive CUDA taxonomy.

claims.original_excerpt: Runtime submission layer — kernel launch and dependency scheduling
claims.finding: Submission and scheduling are useful concepts; some scheduling also occurs on device.

claims.original_excerpt: Kernel boundary — each individual global function launch
claims.finding: A kernel launch creates a grid; dependencies and execution scope matter more than a four-layer classification.

claims.original_excerpt: In-kernel execution — threads, warps, shared memory, registers
claims.finding: Correct examples of device execution and storage concepts.

claims.original_excerpt: CUDA Graph -> runtime submission layer
claims.finding: Also affects device dispatch; graph nodes and dependencies expose a complete workflow to CUDA.

claims.original_excerpt: MegaKernels -> kernel boundary and in-kernel layers
claims.finding: Correct conceptual emphasis, with explicit dependency and resource management.

claims.original_excerpt: The normal way to run GPU code is to submit kernels one at a time from the CPU.
claims.finding: Describes conventional host stream launches; CUDA also supports graph and device-side launch mechanisms.

claims.original_excerpt: Each submission goes through the CUDA driver and lands on a GPU stream.
claims.finding: Describe runtime/driver submission without asserting a distinct direct driver transition per framework operation.

claims.original_excerpt: it triggers the entire workflow at once
claims.finding: One replay enqueues a workflow; nodes execute when their dependencies permit, not simultaneously.

claims.original_excerpt: reducing the idle time ("jitter") between kernels
claims.finding: Can reduce submission and dispatch gaps; jitter specifically means variability and is not a synonym for all idle time.

claims.original_excerpt: about 2.1 us on a regular stream, and about 1.3 us with CUDA Graph replay
claims.finding: Attributed dummy-kernel observation; distinguish the observed device idle/setup interval from CPU API return time.

claims.original_excerpt: That's 38% decrease.
claims.finding: (2.1−1.3)/2.1 = 38.095%; a reduction in that reported overhead, not end-to-end model latency.

claims.original_excerpt: do not: Fuse kernels
claims.finding: Replay does not itself fuse kernel bodies. Framework compilation may fuse before capture.

claims.original_excerpt: Eliminate global-memory traffic between kernels
claims.finding: Replay does not automatically remove the captured kernels' intermediate accesses.

claims.original_excerpt: Remove kernel-boundary synchronization
claims.finding: Default completion edges preserve ordering; graphs can also encode PDL programmatic edges. Avoid an unconditional prohibition.

claims.original_excerpt: Keep intermediate data in registers across kernels
claims.finding: No general register handoff across separate kernels.

claims.original_excerpt: Each kernel inside a CUDA Graph is still an independent kernel.
claims.finding: Separate kernel nodes remain distinct kernels, but they can have explicit dependencies. A graph also has non-kernel node types.

claims.original_excerpt: The graph makes dispatching cheaper.
claims.finding: Can amortize setup and improve repeated dispatch; retain the setup costs and measured scope.

claims.original_excerpt: can launch a dependent kernel early so it can do independent work sooner
claims.finding: Supported on compute capability 9.0+. Concurrent execution is opportunistic.

claims.original_excerpt: dependent work still has to synchronize (cudaGridDependencySynchronize) before consuming producer results
claims.finding: The required data-availability check applies; the guide also permits other means of verification. Never rely on concurrent progress.

claims.original_excerpt: this can still leave pipeline stalls for fine-grained dependencies
claims.finding: A possibility, not an invariant measured PDL cost.

claims.original_excerpt: Three overhead sources stack at each boundary
claims.finding: They may matter and overlap; do not treat them as three independent additive constants.

claims.original_excerpt: 1.3-2.1 us of scheduling overhead
claims.finding: Do not reuse one microbenchmark as a universal scheduling cost.

claims.original_excerpt: With in-order execution on a stream, boundaries force whole-kernel completion semantics.
claims.finding: Correct for ordinary ordered launches; mention PDL and separate-stream concurrency.

claims.original_excerpt: 512 thread blocks on a 148-SM B200 leaves a partial final wave with only 68/148 SMs active (80 idle)
claims.finding: 512 mod 148 = 68 and 148−68 = 80. This requires an idealized one-resident-block-per-SM wave model; real occupancy and durations vary.

claims.original_excerpt: Intermediate tensors are written to HBM, then read by the next kernel
claims.finding: Use global memory; L2 may serve the accesses. DRAM traffic requires counters rather than an assumption.

claims.original_excerpt: Even with PDL-style overlap, dependent sections still wait on data visibility/completion.
claims.finding: Data dependencies still require correctness synchronization.

claims.original_excerpt: around ~100 kernels for Llama-1B forward
claims.finding: Keep attribution, model/configuration, and date; not a timeless launch count for every serving stack.

claims.original_excerpt: ~130 us of launch overhead per forward pass as a back-of-the-envelope estimate
claims.finding: 100×1.3 = 130 µs, but this transfers a dummy-kernel observation. It is not a validated model-runtime decomposition; remove from the main argument.

claims.original_excerpt: vLLM/SGLang reaching only ~50% of available H100 memory bandwidth in this workload
claims.finding: Historical attributed result, not a statement about current versions or an independently reproduced counter measurement.

claims.original_excerpt: one global CUDA function that executes what would traditionally be many kernels
claims.finding: A useful working definition; persistent execution and large fusion are related rather than universally identical terms.

claims.original_excerpt: kernel_1: RMSNorm ... kernel_5: RMSNorm + MLP
claims.finding: Illustrative partition only; actual stacks fuse and split these operations differently.

claims.original_excerpt: removes inter-kernel boundaries and their associated launch/tail/bubble overhead
claims.finding: Removes those launches; reducing tail and pipeline costs requires a suitable internal schedule and communication design.

claims.original_excerpt: For a 16-layer Llama-1B path ... ~100 boundaries removed
claims.finding: A rough configuration-specific scale. K separate launches fused to one removes K−1 inter-launch boundaries; do not present an exact count without a trace.

claims.original_excerpt: Fusing 2-3 ops is standard fusion. Fusing ~100 ops is a different problem.
claims.finding: Useful scale intuition, not a formal threshold between fusion and megakernels.

claims.original_excerpt: A common pattern is an on-GPU interpreter
claims.finding: Established for the cited Hazy designs; neither all fused kernels nor all persistent kernels require an interpreter.

claims.original_excerpt: each SM executes a precomputed instruction stream
claims.finding: Specific to Hazy's scheduling design; CUDA ordinarily assigns blocks to SMs, not one abstract interpreter per SM by definition.

claims.original_excerpt: Schedule construction happens on CPU once and is reused.
claims.finding: Schedules can be reused; input shape, batch composition, and runtime work can require updates or dynamic scheduling.

claims.original_excerpt: provides the low-level kernel framework used by Hazy's MegaKernel work
claims.finding: Supported by the official repositories and ThunderMLA implementation description.

claims.original_excerpt: 20-35% faster than DeepSeek FlashMLA across tested workloads
claims.finding: Headline range, not every reported case: the same post includes a 7.6% speedup case and uses throughput-style speedup percentages. Use case-specific time ratios.

claims.original_excerpt: 41 us vs 52 us on SXM H100
claims.finding: Verified representative configuration. 21.15% latency reduction; 52/41 = 1.2683× speedup. Include prompt lengths, query count, and tensor parallelism.

claims.original_excerpt: full Llama-3.2-1B forward megakernel
claims.finding: Scope remains the cited single-sequence 16-bit inference experiment, not arbitrary models or training.

claims.original_excerpt: 78% memory bandwidth utilization and over 1.5x speedup vs baselines on H100
claims.finding: Keep historical attribution and workload. The reported baseline comparisons differ; not a generic expected speedup.

claims.original_excerpt: code is open-sourced
claims.finding: The official Hazy Megakernels repository is accessible.

claims.original_excerpt: mega-kernelizes PyTorch programs with a few lines of code changes
claims.finding: Author-reported interface for supported models/configurations, not a guarantee for arbitrary PyTorch programs.

claims.original_excerpt: up to 1.0-1.7x latency improvement vs vLLM/SGLang
claims.finding: Use the paper's 1.0–1.7× single-batch serving-performance range; say up to 1.7×, not up to a range. Keep evaluation scope.

claims.original_excerpt: Qwen3-8B on A100 from 14.5 ms to 12.5 ms per-token decode latency
claims.finding: Present in v1 and v2 §6.3; 13.79% latency reduction and 1.16× speedup. This system-level result has multiple causes.

claims.original_excerpt: CUDA Graphs eliminate: CPU submission overhead per kernel
claims.finding: Graphs amortize per-node host work into replay, which still has nonzero enqueue and device costs.

claims.original_excerpt: Kernel boundary setup/teardown overhead
claims.finding: Eliminates repeated launches across fused stages; one launch and internal task transitions remain.

claims.original_excerpt: Cross-kernel tail effects
claims.finding: Can avoid whole-kernel waits for unrelated ready work; remaining load imbalance and the final tail are not erased.

claims.original_excerpt: Full intermediate round-trips between separately launched kernels
claims.finding: Only eliminated for values actually kept local/reused. Cross-block communication may remain global; separate accesses may hit cache.

claims.original_excerpt: Many memory-pipeline bubbles caused by kernel boundaries
claims.finding: Possible when an implementation actually pipelines stages; requires evidence from the chosen schedule.

claims.original_excerpt: megakernels win by improving memory behavior. True in many cases.
claims.finding: Replace an unquantified prevalence claim with specific mechanisms and measured examples.

claims.original_excerpt: asynchronous barrier overhead around ~60 ns each
claims.finding: Hazy's observed low-level overhead on its B200 implementation, not a universal CUDA primitive latency.

claims.original_excerpt: sync plus setup/other overhead summing to about ~120 us
claims.finding: 40+80 = 120 µs in the 600-µs B200 breakdown. Original paragraph omits the architecture and nearby context suggests H100.

claims.original_excerpt: megakernels do not remove all global-memory traffic
claims.finding: Correct; storage and synchronization follow the implementation and dependency scope.

claims.original_excerpt: Large cross-SM dependencies and broad reductions still require global-memory communication.
claims.finding: Often true for these implementations; cluster/distributed shared-memory and cooperative mechanisms make 'require' too universal.

claims.original_excerpt: What they remove is the repeated boundary-induced waste
claims.finding: Launches are removed; costs can reappear as internal communication, scheduling, or resource pressure.

claims.original_excerpt: A megakernel can be launched via CUDA Graphs.
claims.finding: It can be a kernel node, subject to normal capture/graph restrictions.

claims.original_excerpt: if ... one kernel, graph benefit is usually small
claims.finding: Plausible workload hypothesis, not an established universal rule. Measure the one-kernel stream/graph pair.

claims.original_excerpt: CUDA Graph value remains highest when many kernel boundaries still exist.
claims.finding: Topology, host work, setup amortization, and node costs matter; launch count alone cannot rank graph benefit.

claims.original_excerpt: Minimal code changes; Keeps modular kernels; Native support in common stacks; Easier debugging/maintenance
claims.finding: Graphs preserve kernel modularity, but capture-safe control flow, memory lifetime, changing parameters, and debugging can require engineering. Minimal/easier are context-dependent judgments.

claims.original_excerpt: Removes cross-kernel tail effects; Enables deeper cross-op pipelining; Raises bandwidth utilization; Can reduce per-token latency
claims.finding: These are opportunities under suitable implementation/workload conditions, not guaranteed properties of a single launch.

claims.original_excerpt: Harder to implement/debug; Portability/tuning ... harder; Synchronization mistakes ... dangerous; bottlenecks ... shift
claims.finding: Reasonable engineering considerations; present them as tradeoffs rather than measured universal comparisons.

claims.original_excerpt: For most teams: start with CUDA Graphs, profile, then invest ... only if boundary overhead is clearly dominant.
claims.finding: Keep profiling as guidance. Avoid an unsupported claim about most teams or a rule excluding fusion benefits from memory reuse.

claims.original_excerpt: CUDA Graphs = better dispatching. Same stations, cheaper scheduling.
claims.finding: Useful mnemonic, but it omits device scheduling, DAG concurrency, and non-kernel nodes.

claims.original_excerpt: Megakernels = express route. Remove stops between segments.
claims.finding: Can remove external boundaries while retaining internal waits. Replace with the precise implementation comparison.

claims.original_excerpt: Both reduce end-to-end time
claims.finding: Both can reduce time; either can fail to improve or regress a workload.

claims.original_excerpt: CUDA Graphs and megakernels are not substitutes for the same thing.
claims.finding: They change different aspects and can combine, while both may reduce some overlapping launch/dispatch overhead.

claims.original_excerpt: Choosing well starts with identifying which execution layer is actually bottlenecking
claims.finding: Retain as practical advice, with measurement scope and actual implementation evidence.
